questions.q: Complete: public goods are non-excludable and non-________.
questions.fb: Public goods are non-excludable (nobody can be stopped using them) and non-rival (one person's use does not reduce what is left for others). See section 1.

questions.q: Complete: people who enjoy a public good without paying are called ________ riders.
questions.fb: The free rider problem means a private firm cannot charge, so it cannot profit and will not supply the good. See section 1.

questions.q: Why is a street light a public good?
opts: Nobody can be excluded and one person's use does not reduce others' use
It is always provided free by private firms
Only people who pay can see it
questions.fb: It is non-excludable and non-rival. Both characteristics are needed. See section 1.
questions.model: Nobody can be excluded and one person's use does not reduce others' use

questions.q: In a free market, merit goods are likely to be:
questions.fb: Consumers do not fully realise the benefits, so too little is consumed. Healthcare and education are the standard examples. See section 3.

questions.q: In a free market, demerit goods are likely to be:
questions.fb: Consumers lack full information about the harm, so too much is consumed. Cigarettes are the standard example. See section 2.

questions.q: Which of these is a merit good?
questions.fb: Education is more beneficial than consumers realise. Cigarettes are demerit, and street lighting is a public good. See sections 1 to 3.

questions.q: Why might a government set a minimum price for wheat?
opts: To support farmers' incomes and food supply
To help consumers buy it more cheaply
To remove the need for farmers
To cut the cost of imports to zero
questions.fb: Farm incomes are unpredictable because supply is uncertain, and governments want to rely less on imports of staples. See section 4.
questions.model: To support farmers' incomes and food supply

questions.q: Complete: market failure is an inefficient allocation of ________.
questions.fb: Market failure means the price mechanism fails to take account of all costs and benefits, so resources are allocated inefficiently. See 'The big idea'.

opts: Consumers lack the information they need to decide well
The government has too much information
questions.fb: It describes consumers lacking information, which helps explain under-consumption of merit goods and over-consumption of demerit goods. See the Learn tab.
questions.model: Consumers lack the information they need to decide well

questions.q: If a question asks WHY a government intervenes, which is the best type of point to make?
opts: Describe how a tax shifts supply
List the costs of a buffer stock
questions.fb: Reasons relate to market failure. Taxes, subsidies and provision are methods and belong in answers about how. See the 'Reasons, not methods' box.
